title: Preventing miscarriage through platform testing of multiple novel interventions
official: PREMIS: Preventing miscarriage through platform testing of multiple (novel) interventions. Intervention 1: DHA trial: Docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) (omega-3) to improve live birth rate in women with previous miscarriage
summary:
Background and study aims
Omega-3 fatty acids play a crucial role in modulating factors linked to the origin and development of recurrent miscarriage, including immune cell dysregulation, oxidative stress, and inflammation. Long-chain polyunsaturated fatty acids (LCPUFAs), specifically docosahexaenoic acid (DHA) and eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), play a vital role in gestational health, particularly in influencing gestational length in singleton pregnancies. Studies have shown that adequate intake of these fatty acids during pregnancy is associated with a reduced risk of preterm birth and may promote longer gestation periods.

Miscarriage and preterm birth share several common causes, including inflammation, which can adversely affect pregnancy outcomes. Given these shared causes, interventions designed to prevent preterm birth—such as nutritional supplementation, lifestyle modifications, and pharmacological therapies—could also prove beneficial in reducing the risk of miscarriage.

It remains unknown whether DHA deficiency or insufficiency reduces the risk of miscarriage. At the moment, there are no strategies in the NHS in the UK to increase DHA levels and potentially reduce the risk of miscarriage. The study's definitive primary objective is to test the hypothesis that DHA supplementation at two different doses, used alone, increases the rate of live birth ≥ 34 weeks of gestation by at least 8% in women who have experienced two or more miscarriages. The intermediate primary objective is to test the hypothesis that DHA supplementation at two different doses, used alone, increases the rate of ongoing pregnancy, at 11-14 weeks, by at least 10% in women who have experienced two or more miscarriages.

Who can participate?
Females aged 16 years or over who have experienced two or more previous miscarriages, actively trying to become pregnant, and have confirmation of positive pregnancy test

What does the study involve? 
Participants will be randomly assigned to one of three groups:

Control group: no DHA (omega 3)
Low dose group: 750 mg of (omega 3) DHA per day
High dose group: 1125 mg of (omega 3) DHA per day

The low dose will be taken as two capsules daily, and the high dose as three capsules daily, both taken by mouth until 24 weeks of pregnancy.
These doses were chosen based on a thorough review of existing research and the known safety of the supplement. Because there is variation in the evidence about the best amount of DHA to take during pregnancy, the study will test both the low and high dose options.

What are the possible benefits and risks of participating? 
Despite the benefits, many pregnant individuals do not consume sufficient levels of DHA and EPA, highlighting the need for increased awareness and potential dietary interventions to optimise pregnancy outcomes. The participants randomised to receive the omega-3 supplements will be provided with omega-3 supplements at no cost and as part of the care pathway.

There are no known risks to taking DHA (omega-3) supplements. However, any queries that arise may be discussed with the participants local care team. 

Where is the study run from?  
University of Birmingham, UK

When is the study starting and how long is it expected to run for? 
August 2026 to May 2030

Who is funding the study? 
Tommy's Charity, UK

Who is the main contact?
Mr Lee Priest, Research Fellow/Team Leader, l.priest.1@bham.ac.uk, premis@trials.bham.ac.uk

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
1.	Written informed consent to receive DHA (omega-3) supplements
2.	Patient confirmation of positive pregnancy test 
3.	Fish consumption - 0, 1 or 2 portions per week (1 portion defined as 140g or 4.9oz when cooked)
Exclusion criteria:
1. Currently taking omega-3 supplementation with DHA concentration >300mg and unwilling to stop
2. Sensitive or allergic to fish or seafood
